title: Four sides
hookLine: Methodists speak of scripture, tradition, reason and experience working together

lines: A RIDER WITH SADDLEBAGS OF BOOKS.
cards: A rider on a country road in England, saddlebags heavy with books, heading for the next village to preach in a field.
Day eight hundred ninety-five met him: John Wesley, an Anglican priest whose followers became the Methodists. Tradition says he read on horseback. He argued with friends by letter.

And when a hard question came up, he didn't reach for just one thing. Methodists still speak of the habit he left them: four things, working together. Today's word is the shape of that habit: four sides.

teach.b: The four sides are scripture, tradition, reason and experience. Scripture comes first. A psalm says: "Thy word is a lamp unto my feet, and a light unto my path."
A lamp shows the next step, and Methodists start there. Then tradition: what the church has said and prayed before you arrived.
Jeremiah has the line: "ask for the old paths, where is the good way, and walk therein." Creeds, old teachers and hymns are a kind of old path. Then reason.

teach.h: COME NOW, AND LET US REASON.
teach.b: In Isaiah, God says: "Come now, and let us reason together." In this picture, thinking carefully isn't the enemy of faith; it's part of it. And last, experience.
Wesley wrote in his journal about an evening meeting in London when, as he put it, his heart was strangely warmed, and he felt sure he was forgiven.
Paul says something close: "The Spirit itself beareth witness with our spirit, that we are the children of God." A witness from the inside. Now the careful part.
Methodist teachers say the four sides are not equal votes. Scripture is the ground; the other three help you read it, test your reading, and live it.
The name for the pattern came later, from teachers looking back at how Wesley worked. And the sides check each other. A warm feeling that contradicts scripture gets questioned.
A reading no one in the church has ever held gets a second look. A neat argument that crushes real people's lives gets tested against what has actually happened to them.

how: Methodist churches teach that scripture is the primary source of faith, read with the help of tradition, reason and experience, and some study groups think a question through by asking what each of the four sides says.

o: four rules for how a Methodist service runs
scripture, tradition, reason and experience together
four Gospels read side by side for one story

games.q: the four sides — tap the pairs.
p: come now, and let us reason together

s: in the Methodist picture, the four sides are equal votes
Methodist teachers say scripture is the ground; the other three help read it, test it and live it.
experience is one of the four sides
Wesley wrote of his heart being strangely warmed, and Paul of the Spirit bearing witness with our spirit.
reason is treated as the enemy of faith
Isaiah has God say, "come now, and let us reason together."

games.q: you've had a strong, warm feeling that something is true, but it seems to go against scripture. in the Methodist picture, what happens next?
o: the feeling wins; it came from inside.
the feeling gets questioned against scripture.
you drop scripture and follow reason alone.
games.why: the sides check each other, and scripture is the ground. experience matters, which is why Wesley wrote about his warmed heart, but it gets tested, not crowned.

practice: Pick one thing you hold true about God or about how to live, and walk slowly around it: what scripture says, as far as you know; what the church has said before; whether it makes sense when you think it through; how it has gone in your own life.
Notice which side feels solid, and which you've never checked. If you pray, you can ask for light on that side.

wordCard.voice: Four sides. Scripture, tradition, reason and experience: the Methodist way of turning a question of faith all the way round, with scripture as the ground.

orig.note: Greek, Romans 8:16: bears witness with. the Spirit and our spirit, two witnesses together.

carryVoice: Your line: four sides of a question. Scripture stays the ground. That's today, done.
